issues.legal_issue: An application describing limestone as being for burning purposes and identifying the intended minerals as minor minerals is an application for a minor-mineral lease when its terms are read as a whole.
material_facts: The applicant sought a quarry lease for limestone for burning purposes and identified the intended minerals as minor minerals.
A related application for the same area sought a mining lease for limestone as a major mineral.
The application’s wording was materially similar to the application considered in an earlier Supreme Court decision.
issues.conclusion: The application and the lease granted on it were for limestone as a minor mineral; the contrary classification by the Central Government and High Court was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, the classification of a mineral depends on the Central Government’s notification. Following Smt. Rukmani Bai Gupta v. State Government of Madhya Pradesh, the application must be read as a whole; its references to limestone for burning purposes and to minor minerals together showed that it sought a minor-mineral lease.

predicates.mineral_lease_classification_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal disputing whether an application for a mineral lease was for a minor or major mineral.
predicates.application_describes_limestone_for_burn: The applicant describes the limestone sought as being for burning purposes.
predicates.application_identifies_minor_minerals: The applicant identifies minor minerals as the minerals intended to be extracted.

issues.definition: When a mineral-lease classification appeal concerns an application that describes limestone for burning and identifies minor minerals, the application is for a minor mineral.

issues.legal_issue: Under the narrower category introduced by the later notification, limestone is a minor mineral only if it is suitable for kiln burning to produce lime ordinarily usable as building material.
material_facts: The Central Government’s 1958 notification covered limestone used for lime burning irrespective of the burning process or the quality of lime produced.
The 1961 notification narrowed the category to limestone used in kilns to manufacture lime used as building material.
The Court noted that inferior-grade limestone was ordinarily used to produce building-material lime, while superior-grade limestone was ordinarily used for other purposes.
issues.conclusion: Under the later notification, only limestone capable of being used in kilns to produce lime ordinarily usable as building material is a minor mineral; the earlier notification had covered limestone used for lime burning without that limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Applying section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, and the 1958 and 1961 notifications, the Court followed and clarified Smt. Rukmani Bai Gupta v. State Government of Madhya Pradesh: the later notification narrowed the limestone category by requiring kiln burning and the production of building-material quality lime.

predicates.limestone_classification_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether limestone falls within a minor-mineral category.
predicates.limestone_suitable_for_kiln_burning_to_m: The limestone is capable of being burned in kilns to produce lime ordinarily usable as building material.

issues.definition: In a limestone-classification proceeding, limestone suitable for kiln burning to make building-material lime falls within the minor-mineral category.

issues.legal_issue: A lessee’s responsibility under the narrower limestone category ends when the quarried limestone is used in kilns to produce building-material quality lime, without requiring the lessee to control the lime’s eventual use.
material_facts: The later notification covered limestone used in kilns to manufacture lime used as building material.
The Court reasoned that a lessee could control the use of quarried limestone in the relevant burning process but could not control whether the resulting lime was actually used as building material.
issues.conclusion: The lessee’s responsibility ceases once the limestone is used in kilns to produce building-material quality lime; the lessee need not ensure that the resulting lime is actually used as building material.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted the 1961 notification under section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, and followed Smt. Rukmani Bai Gupta v. State Government of Madhya Pradesh in distinguishing the required process and quality of the product from the lessee’s control over its ultimate use.

predicates.limestone_lease_classification_proceedin: The proceeding concerns a lessee’s responsibilities under a limestone lease.
predicates.quarried_limestone_is_used_in_kilns_to_p: The lessee’s quarried limestone is used in kilns to produce lime of a quality ordinarily usable as building material.

issues.definition: In a limestone-lease proceeding, a lessee’s responsibility ends once the quarried limestone is used in kilns to produce building-material quality lime.

issues.legal_issue: When competing applicants seek leases over the same area on the basis that its limestone is respectively a minor or major mineral, the State must consider both applications and determine the proper lease category by assessing the quality of the limestone in the area.
material_facts: One applicant sought a quarry lease for limestone as a minor mineral, while another sought a mining lease for limestone as a major mineral over the same area.
The State granted the minor-mineral lease without considering the competing major-mineral application.
The Central Government directed consideration of only the major-mineral application.
The record did not permit the Court to determine whether the area’s limestone was predominantly of a quality suitable for minor-mineral use or was high-grade limestone.
issues.conclusion: Neither application could properly be ignored. The State was directed to consider both applications, assess the quality of the limestone in the area, and grant the appropriate type of lease according to that assessment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the grant must reflect the quality of the limestone in the area: if its major portion is suitable for minor-mineral use, a lease under the State rules is appropriate; if its major portion is high-grade limestone, a lease under the Central rules is appropriate. A special lease condition may address occasional limestone of a different grade. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this competing-applications ruling.

predicates.competing_lease_grant_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the grant of a mineral lease where competing applications are before the decision-maker.
predicates.applicants_seek_different_mineral_classi: Applicants seek leases for the same area on the basis that its mineral is respectively a minor or major mineral.
predicates.area_quality_determines_appropriate_leas: The quality of the mineral in the area determines which type of lease is appropriate.

issues.definition: When competing applicants seek different mineral classifications for the same area and area quality determines the proper lease category, the State must assess both applications and the area quality before granting a lease.

issues.legal_issue: Royalty for extracted limestone is payable at the rate applicable to the mineral classification of the lease under which it was extracted.
material_facts: The Court held that the first applicant’s application and lease concerned limestone as a minor mineral.
The competing applicant held a mining lease for limestone as a major mineral during part of the relevant period.
Both applicants had extracted limestone under their respective leases.
The first applicant offered to withdraw two royalty-related writ petitions and pay the demanded sum if his lease was held to be for a minor mineral.
issues.conclusion: For the past periods of their respective leases, the first applicant was liable for royalty at the minor-mineral rate and the competing lessee was liable at the major-mineral rate. The Court allowed the State’s appeal concerning the royalty writ orders and permitted those writ petitions to be withdrawn.
issues.legal_principle: Royalty liability followed the classification of the mineral under the relevant lease: the first applicant’s lease was for a minor mineral, while the competing lessee’s was for a major mineral. The Court did not cite a separate statutory provision or earlier case for this royalty ruling.

predicates.mineral_lease_royalty_proceeding: The proceeding concerns royalty payable for minerals extracted under a lease.
predicates.mineral_extracted_under_lease: The lessee extracted mineral under the lease during the period in question.
predicates.lease_mineral_classification_is_determin: The mineral classification applicable to the lease has been determined.

issues.definition: In a royalty proceeding, when mineral has been extracted under a lease and the lease’s mineral classification is determined, royalty is payable at the rate for that classification.
